title: Soviet troops storm Kabul
what: Soviet forces took key points in Kabul from 25 December, and on the 27th they stormed the palace of Afghanistan's president Hafizullah Amin, who was killed. Moscow installed Babrak Karmal in his place; some 30,000 Soviet troops were sent. Washington calls it a grave threat to peace; how the West will answer is not yet clear.
why: The opening move of the Cold War's last decade: it ends detente, brings the grain embargo and the Olympic boycott, and feeds the fear that sends gold to its 1980 peak. The Soviet Union will spend nine years and much of its strength in Afghanistan.

title: Reagan beats Carter in a landslide
what: Ronald Reagan won the US presidency on 4 November with 489 electoral votes to 49 and about 51 percent of the vote to Carter's 41, carrying 44 states. He promises tax cuts, less regulation and a harder line with Moscow. Shares jumped: the day after the vote the New York Stock Exchange traded a record 84 million shares, and the Dow climbed back above 1,000 for the first time since 1976. On 20 November the S&P 500 closed at a record 140.40, and it gained 10% in the month.
why: Wall Street's verdict on the new president was a +10% month, one of the best of the decade; Reagan's tax cuts, deregulation and arms build-up frame the 1980s market, though the first two years bring recession under Volcker's high rates.

title: Martial law in Poland
what: General Wojciech Jaruzelski, Poland's Communist Party leader and defence minister, declared martial law on 13 December. Thousands of activists of Solidarity, the free trade union born in the Gdansk shipyard strikes of August 1980, were locked up without trial, among them its leader Lech Walesa; telephone lines were cut, borders and airports closed, and a curfew runs from 7 in the evening to 6 in the morning. On 16 December security forces killed 9 striking miners at the Wujek coal mine. On 23 December the United States imposed economic sanctions on the Polish government.
why: The Soviet bloc crushes its first free movement, and Reagan answers with sanctions; Solidarity survives underground and wins the free election of June 1989 that starts the year of revolutions.

title: Argentina seizes the Falkland Islands; Britain sends a fleet
what: On 2 April Argentina, ruled by a military junta under General Galtieri, invaded the Falkland Islands in the South Atlantic, a British colony since 1841 that Argentina claims as its own. Britain's prime minister Margaret Thatcher answered at once: on 5 April aircraft carriers left Portsmouth at the head of a task force that will grow to 127 ships, on their way to take the islands back.
why: A short war that fills the news of spring 1982: Argentina surrenders on 14 June after 74 days and about 900 dead; the junta falls a year later, and Thatcher wins re-election.

title: A million people march against the bomb
what: On 12 June about one million people filled the streets of New York to demand an end to the arms race, the largest peace rally in American history. The United States and the Soviet Union each keep enough nuclear missiles to destroy the other even after being attacked first, so neither could win a war: the idea is called 'mutual assured destruction', MAD for short. At the last count the Soviet Union had about 30,000 nuclear warheads and the United States 23,000. Together they have the force of more than a million Hiroshima bombs, far more than it would take to destroy every city on Earth: people call it 'overkill'. The marchers want a 'freeze': both sides should stop building, testing and deploying new weapons.
why: Makes the nuclear threat of the Cold War felt: the size of the arsenals, MAD and overkill. The warhead counts are those of 1980; the freeze won referendums in nine states that November.
changed: Cold War storyline: new beat on the nuclear threat (MAD, overkill, size of the arsenals); June 1982 had no news

title: Reagan's 'evil empire' and a shield in space
what: On 8 March President Reagan told a meeting of evangelical Christians in Orlando that the Soviet Union is 'the focus of evil in the modern world'. On 23 March, in a televised address, he called on American scientists to give the country the means of rendering nuclear missiles 'impotent and obsolete' with a defence, partly based in space, that could destroy them in flight. Senator Edward Kennedy mocked it as 'reckless Star Wars schemes', and the name Star Wars has stuck.
why: The peak of Reagan's build-up and rhetoric. Moscow could not afford to match the Strategic Defense Initiative, and SDI becomes the sticking point at Reykjavik in 1986.

title: The new American missiles arrive in Europe
what: The first US cruise missiles arrived at RAF Greenham Common in England on 13 November, and the first Pershing II launchers reached West Germany later in the month. NATO decided in 1979 to station the missiles unless the Soviet Union scrapped its SS-20s; after the first Pershings arrived, the Soviet Union broke off the Geneva talks on medium-range weapons. Peace protesters have camped outside Greenham Common since 1981, and in April some 70,000 people formed a human chain there.
why: The low point of the Cold War of the 1980s. The missiles that frightened Europe become the bargaining chip for the INF treaty of 1987.

title: 'Nuclear winter': a nuclear war would darken and freeze the Earth
what: A group of scientists that includes the astronomer Carl Sagan published a study in the journal Science in late December: after a nuclear war, smoke and soot from burning cities would stay in the sky for years, block the sunlight and cool the whole planet. They call it 'nuclear winter'. Harvests would fail everywhere, also in countries that no bomb had hit. A month earlier, on 20 November, about 100 million Americans watched the television film 'The Day After', which shows a town in Kansas after a nuclear attack. In the debate that followed, Sagan compared the two superpowers to enemies standing in a room awash in gasoline, one holding nine thousand matches, the other seven thousand.
why: Introduces 'nuclear winter'. President Reagan wrote in his diary that the film left him 'greatly depressed'; it is one reason why he sought talks with Moscow in his second term.
changed: Cold War storyline: new beat introducing nuclear winter

title: Indira Gandhi is assassinated
what: On 31 October India's prime minister Indira Gandhi was shot dead at her home in New Delhi by two of her own bodyguards. They were Sikhs taking revenge: in June she had sent the army into the Golden Temple in Amritsar, the holiest place of the Sikh religion, to drive out armed militants. Her son Rajiv Gandhi has been sworn in as prime minister.
why: The leader of the world's largest democracy is killed; days of deadly riots against Sikhs follow in early November.

title: Reagan re-elected in a 49-state landslide
what: On 6 November Ronald Reagan, 73, won a second term with 525 of 538 electoral votes and 58.8% of the popular vote; Walter Mondale carried only his home state of Minnesota and the District of Columbia. Mondale had made history by choosing Geraldine Ferraro as his running mate, the first woman on a major party ticket. With inflation down to about 4% and the economy growing fast, "Morning in America" was an easy sell.
why: Every presidential election gets a beat (curator rule). The margin is the biggest in electoral votes ever.

title: Gorbachev takes over the Soviet Union
what: Mikhail Gorbachev, 54, was chosen on 11 March as general secretary of the Soviet Communist Party, a day after Konstantin Chernenko died. He follows three old and sick leaders who died within two and a half years: Brezhnev, Andropov and Chernenko. The West is trying to work out what the new man wants.
why: The man who ends the Cold War: perestroika and glasnost, the arms treaties, letting eastern Europe go in 1989, and finally the end of the Soviet Union in 1991.

title: Reagan and Gorbachev meet in Geneva
what: US President Ronald Reagan and Soviet leader Mikhail Gorbachev met in Geneva from 19 to 21 November, the first US-Soviet summit since 1979. They agreed on no arms cuts, but their joint statement says a nuclear war cannot be won and must never be fought, and they agreed to meet again.
why: A Swiss stage for the thaw; the personal trust built here leads through Reykjavik to the INF treaty.

title: People power: Filipinos drive out their dictator
what: Ferdinand Marcos, who has ruled the Philippines for about twenty years, claimed victory in the election of 7 February, but independent poll watchers counted his rival Corazon Aquino ahead, and thirty of the officials' own computer operators walked out in protest at the cheating. From 22 to 25 February more than two million people filled a main avenue of Manila, backed by the Catholic Church. Marcos and his family fled to Hawaii, and Aquino, widow of an opposition leader murdered in 1983, is president.
why: A peaceful revolution, three years before those of eastern Europe: a hopeful story in a month that had none.

title: Chernobyl: a Soviet reactor explodes and a radioactive cloud drifts over Europe
what: In the early hours of 26 April reactor number four of the Chernobyl nuclear power station in Ukraine exploded and burned. The Soviet Union said nothing until 28 April, after radiation alarms went off at a Swedish plant more than 1,000 kilometres away; that evening Moscow admitted "an accident" with "one of the nuclear reactors damaged". The 53,000 people of the plant workers' town, Pripyat, were taken away by bus on 27 April, and a 10-kilometre zone around the plant was emptied. Two workers are known to have died in the explosion; how many are sick from radiation, and how far the fallout reaches, is not yet known.
why: The defining disaster of the decade for Europeans, missing from the first draft of the world arc. Figures as known at the end of April: the 28 radiation deaths of the following months, the 30-kilometre zone (ten days later) and the food restrictions across Europe belong to a May beat. Curator asked for it.

title: After Chernobyl: the zone widens to 30 kilometres, Europe tests its milk and vegetables
what: Ten days after the explosion the evacuation zone around Chernobyl was widened to 30 kilometres, taking some 68,000 more people from their homes; in Kiev the May Day parade went ahead, shortened to under two hours. Across Europe governments measured the fallout and told people what not to eat and drink, from fresh vegetables to milk, with rules differing from one border to the next. Twenty-eight of the plant workers and firemen have died of radiation sickness in the weeks since the fire.
why: The month Europe lived with the cloud; the death toll of 28 within three months is the figure given for 1986. The food-restriction detail is general (sourced only as "countries experienced fallout and restrictions" is not in the fetched page section), so it stays unspecific; a Swiss source on the 1986 measures (BAG, NZZ of 2 June 1986 in the scans) would sharpen it. Review 2026-10: city name as spelled in English at the time.

title: Reykjavik: so close to scrapping the missiles
what: The world has never held more nuclear weapons than now: about 70,000 warheads, some 40,000 of them Soviet and more than 20,000 American. Ronald Reagan and Mikhail Gorbachev met in Reykjavik, Iceland, on 11 and 12 October and talked about cuts no one had expected: Reagan proposed scrapping all ballistic missiles within ten years, and Gorbachev went further and offered to scrap all nuclear weapons within a decade. The talks broke down over Reagan's missile shield, the Strategic Defense Initiative, which Gorbachev wanted confined to laboratory research for ten years. The two leaders went home without an agreement.
why: It looked like failure, but each side learned how far the other would go; fourteen months later the INF treaty is signed, with on-site inspections Moscow had never accepted before.
changed: Cold War storyline: the size of the arsenals at their peak (1986) added

title: Reagan and Gorbachev sign the INF treaty
what: President Reagan and Mikhail Gorbachev signed the Intermediate-Range Nuclear Forces Treaty in Washington on 8 December. It removes all American and Soviet land-based missiles with ranges of 500 to 5,500 kilometres, including the Pershing II and cruise missiles in western Europe and the Soviet SS-20s, with inspections on both sides. At Reykjavik in October 1986 the two leaders had come close to far deeper cuts but parted over Reagan's missile shield. It is the first treaty that makes the arsenals smaller: until now, agreements only slowed their growth to the 70,000 warheads reached last year.
why: The first treaty to abolish a whole class of nuclear weapons; with the crash of October behind them, markets had other worries, but for Europe the missile scare of 1983 is over.
changed: Cold War storyline: look-back to the peak of the arsenals added

title: George Bush wins the White House: "Read my lips, no new taxes"
what: Vice President George Bush won the presidency on 8 November with 426 electoral votes and 53.4% of the vote against Michael Dukakis, the governor of Massachusetts. The campaign was marked by Bush's convention pledge, "Read my lips: no new taxes", and for Dukakis's ride in a tank, which the Bush campaign turned into an attack advertisement. Bush takes over from Reagan in January with the economy in its sixth year of growth.
why: Every presidential election gets a beat (curator rule). The tax pledge sets up 1990 and 1992. Review 2026-10: 'is remembered for' was hindsight.

title: The last Soviet soldiers leave Afghanistan
what: On 15 February the last Soviet military column left Afghanistan, crossing the Friendship Bridge at Termez into Soviet Uzbekistan; its commander, General Boris Gromov, crossed last. The withdrawal, agreed in the Geneva Accords of April 1988, began in May, and half the troops were gone by August. In more than nine years of war thousands of Soviet soldiers and hundreds of thousands of Afghans have died, and some five million Afghans have fled abroad, most of them to Pakistan and Iran. The Afghan government of Najibullah fights on with Soviet aid.
why: The war that opened the decade ends in a Soviet retreat, a sign that Gorbachev will no longer hold on by force; nine months later the Wall opens.

title: East Germans flee to the West through Hungary
what: East Germany does not let its people travel to the West: a wall and a guarded border keep them in. But Hungary, another communist country, began taking down its border fence with Austria on 2 May, and on 19 August several hundred East Germans on holiday there rushed through a gate opened for a picnic at the border. Since 10 September Hungary lets all East Germans cross into Austria freely. At home, people in Leipzig have gathered every Monday since 4 September to demand change, despite arrests and beatings.
why: The crack in the Iron Curtain: without it the opening of the Berlin Wall in November comes out of nowhere.

title: The Berlin Wall opens
what: On the evening of 9 November an East German spokesman, Guenter Schabowski, announced at a press conference that citizens could cross the border, effective immediately as he understood it; that night crowds pushed through the checkpoints in Berlin and the guards gave way. It follows a year of change in eastern Europe, with free elections in Poland in June and Hungary opening its border. On 17 November mass protests began in Czechoslovakia.
why: The defining moment of the arc. German shares were among the strongest in the game over the next two months (Siemens +21% in November, Daimler-Benz +34% in December) on hopes for a market of 17 million new customers, though the move is not tied to a cited report here.

title: Revolutions sweep the rest of eastern Europe
what: Presidents Bush and Gorbachev met off Malta on 2 and 3 December. In Prague the communists gave up power after weeks of peaceful protest, and the dissident playwright Vaclav Havel was elected president on 29 December. In Romania an uprising that began in Timisoara on 16 December reached Bucharest, and the dictator Nicolae Ceausescu was executed on 25 December.
why: Within a year the Soviet empire in Europe is gone; the 1990s open with a peace dividend and new markets in the East.

title: Germany is one country again
what: At midnight on 3 October the German Democratic Republic joined the Federal Republic and Germany was reunited, eleven months after the Wall opened. The Two Plus Four treaty, signed in Moscow on 12 September by the two German states and the four wartime Allies, restores Germany's full sovereignty. On 20 September both German parliaments approved the unification treaty by large majorities.
why: Unification's cost, high German interest rates, and the European response to a bigger Germany (Maastricht and the euro) shape the next decade in Europe.

title: Hardliners try a coup in Moscow and fail
what: On 19 August eight hardliners, among them Vice President Gennady Yanayev, KGB chief Vladimir Kryuchkov and Defence Minister Dmitry Yazov, announced that they had taken power, saying Mikhail Gorbachev was unable to govern; he was held at his holiday home in Crimea, a day before he was to sign a new union treaty giving the republics more power. Tanks came into Moscow, but Russia's president Boris Yeltsin climbed onto one outside the Russian parliament and called for resistance; three civilians were killed on 21 August, and the coup collapsed. Gorbachev gave up the leadership of the Communist Party on 24 August, the day Ukraine declared independence; Estonia and Latvia had declared theirs during the coup.
why: The coup meant to save the Soviet Union destroys it: power passes to Yeltsin and the republics, and the union is dissolved four months later.

title: The Soviet Union ceases to exist
what: The leaders of Russia, Ukraine and Belarus declared on 8 December that the Soviet Union no longer exists and founded a Commonwealth of Independent States, which eight more republics joined on 21 December. Mikhail Gorbachev resigned on 25 December and handed the nuclear codes to Boris Yeltsin; the red flag was lowered over the Kremlin, and the Soviet Union was formally dissolved the next day.
why: The end of the Cold War that frames the first decade of the game. December's +11% on Wall Street was a Federal Reserve rate cut, not this, but the 1990s peace dividend and globalisation start here.

title: Maastricht: Europe agrees on a single currency
what: At Maastricht on 9 and 10 December the twelve European Community leaders agreed on a treaty for a European Union with common citizenship, foreign policy cooperation and an economic and monetary union with a single currency by 1999 at the latest. Countries must meet limits on inflation, deficits, debt and interest rates to join. The treaty still has to be ratified by all twelve, some by referendum.
why: The blueprint for the euro; its ratification troubles of 1992 and its convergence rules run through the decade.

title: Black Wednesday, and France's narrow yes
what: On 16 September Britain spent billions defending the pound and raised its base rate from 10 to 12 percent, then promised 15, before pulling sterling out of the European exchange-rate mechanism that evening; Italy's lira also left. On 20 September French voters approved the Maastricht treaty by only 51 percent, after Danish voters rejected it in June by 50.7 percent.
why: Europe's currency plan nearly breaks; the episode explains why the euro was built with a hard central bank and why Britain never joined.

title: Clinton wins the White House
what: Bill Clinton, the 46-year-old governor of Arkansas, won the US presidency on 3 November with 370 electoral votes and 43 percent of the vote, against 37.5 percent for President George Bush and 18.9 percent for the independent Ross Perot. The recession has ended, but unemployment remains above 7 percent.
why: Clinton's eight years, with deficit reduction and falling interest rates, coincide with the great bull market of the 1990s.

title: Swiss voters say no to the European Economic Area
what: On 6 December Swiss voters rejected membership of the European Economic Area by 50.3 to 49.7 percent, a margin of about 24,000 votes, on a turnout of 78.7 percent, and a clear majority of the cantons voted no. French-speaking cantons voted strongly yes, German-speaking rural ones strongly no. The government's application to join the European Community, sent in May, is now frozen.
why: The defining Swiss political vote of the game: it sets Switzerland on the bilateral path, makes Christoph Blocher's SVP the country's strongest force, and is a backdrop of the weak Swiss economy of the mid-1990s.

title: Clinton re-elected; Perot takes 8%
what: Bill Clinton won a second term on 5 November with 379 electoral votes and 49.2% of the vote against Bob Dole's 40.7%; Ross Perot, running again as an independent, took 8.4%. The economy is growing, inflation is low and the stock market has doubled since Clinton took office, which left Dole little to run on.
why: Every presidential election gets a beat (curator rule).

title: Eleven countries qualify for the euro; Greece does not
what: On 3 May, at a summit in Brussels, EU leaders chose the eleven countries that will adopt the euro on 1 January 1999: Germany, France, Italy, Spain, the Netherlands, Belgium, Austria, Portugal, Finland, Ireland and Luxembourg. Belgium and Italy were let in although their government debts, about 122 percent of their annual economic output in 1997, are twice the 60 percent limit. Greece failed the tests: its 1997 deficit of 4.0 percent was above the 3 percent limit, and its inflation of 5.4 percent was far too high.
why: The euro's founding compromise: the rules were bent for big debtors, and Greece, kept out now, is let in two years later. Doubts about Greek figures surface in 2004 and explode in 2009.
source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_euro (read 2026-10-04); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euro_convergence_criteria (read 2026-10-04); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enlargement_of_the_eurozone (read 2026-10-04); European Monetary Institute, Convergence Report, March 1998, https://www.ecb.europa.eu/pub/pdf/conrep/cr1998en.pdf (read 2026-10-04)

title: The euro is born
what: On 1 January eleven EU countries, among them Germany, France and Italy, fixed their exchange rates irrevocably and adopted the euro, which now trades on currency markets and is used by banks and bond markets; notes and coins follow in 2002. The European Central Bank in Frankfurt sets one interest rate for all of them. Britain, Sweden and Denmark stay out, and so, of course, does Switzerland.
why: The euro makes Switzerland's neighbours one currency bloc; the franc becomes the haven Europeans run to whenever the euro is in doubt, in 2010-2012 above all.

title: Yeltsin resigns; Putin takes over
what: In a televised New Year's Eve address on 31 December Boris Yeltsin resigned as president of Russia and named his prime minister, Vladimir Putin, as acting president. Putin, a former KGB officer, became prime minister only in August. A presidential election must be held within three months.
why: The start of the Putin era, which leads to Georgia, Crimea and the war of 2022.

title: Swiss voters back the bilateral treaties with the EU
what: On 21 May Swiss voters approved the seven sector agreements with the European Union, Bilaterals I, by 67.2 percent. They cover the free movement of people, land and air transport, trade barriers, farm goods, research and public procurement.
why: The bilateral path is Switzerland's answer to the EEA no and the base of its relations with the EU until today; the free movement of people becomes the political fault line of the 2014 vote.

title: Bush or Gore? America votes and has no winner
what: Americans voted on 7 November, and three weeks later they still do not know who their next president is. Everything hangs on Florida: on election night the television networks called the state for Al Gore, then for George W. Bush, then for nobody, and Gore phoned Bush to concede and took it back. Bush led by 1,784 votes on election night and by 327 after a machine recount; Gore asked for recounts by hand in four counties, where officials now study punch cards that voters did not punch through cleanly. On 26 November Florida declared Bush the winner by 537 votes, and Gore went to court the next day.
why: Every change in the White House gets a beat (curator rule), and this one sets up the Supreme Court's decision in December. The five weeks of uncertainty weighed on a market already falling from the dotcom peak.

title: The Supreme Court decides the election for Bush
what: Five weeks after the vote of 7 November, the US Supreme Court stopped the Florida recount on 12 December in Bush v. Gore, and Al Gore conceded the next day. George W. Bush won Florida by 537 votes and the electoral college by 271 to 266, while Gore won more votes nationwide.
why: Bush's presidency is defined by 9/11 and the wars in Afghanistan and Iraq; the long count added to the nerves of a market already falling from the dotcom peak.

title: Greece becomes the twelfth euro country
what: On 1 January Greece adopted the euro, two years after the first eleven countries. In 1998 it had failed the entry tests; in June 2000 the EU judged that it now meets them and fixed the rate at 340.75 drachmas per euro. Like Italy and Belgium, Greece owes more than its whole annual economic output, far above the 60 percent limit in the rules. Euro notes and coins are to follow in all twelve countries in January 2002.
why: Greece's entry rested on a reported 1999 deficit of 1.8 percent; the 2004 audit put it at 3.4 percent, above the limit. Cheap borrowing in euros then fed the debts that broke out in 2009.
source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enlargement_of_the_eurozone (read 2026-10-04); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euro_convergence_criteria (read 2026-10-04); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_euro (read 2026-10-04); European Monetary Institute, Convergence Report, March 1998, https://www.ecb.europa.eu/pub/pdf/conrep/cr1998en.pdf (read 2026-10-04); Eurostat, Report on the revision of the Greek government deficit and debt figures, 22 November 2004, https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/documents/4187653/5765001/GREECE-EN.PDF (read 2026-10-04)

title: Terror attacks on New York and Washington
what: On 11 September nineteen hijackers seized four airliners; two destroyed the twin towers of the World Trade Center in New York, one hit the Pentagon and one crashed in Pennsylvania, and thousands are dead. Al-Qaeda, led by Osama bin Laden, is blamed; Congress voted 15 billion dollars of aid for the airlines, and NATO invoked its mutual-defence clause for the first time. The New York Stock Exchange stayed closed until 17 September, its longest closure since the Great Depression, and when it reopened the Dow fell 684 points, or 7.1 percent, its largest point fall ever; airline, insurance and travel shares fell hardest, and the S&P 500 lost 8% in September. Boeing, whose jets were used in the attacks, lost 35% and will cut 20,000 to 30,000 airliner jobs as airlines cut flights. Disney, whose parks emptied as air travel stopped, lost 27%, and Siemens lost a quarter of its value.
why: The defining event of the decade's politics; it deepened the recession of 2001, hit Boeing (-35% in the month) and the airlines, and leads to the wars in Afghanistan and Iraq. The final death toll was 2,977 victims.

title: Swissair grounded
what: On 2 October Swissair grounded its entire fleet when fuel suppliers refused to fill its planes without cash and UBS would not release a bridging loan for daily operations; thousands of passengers were stranded around the world. Federal President Moritz Leuenberger called it a disaster and blamed UBS and Credit Suisse for abandoning the airline, and angry crowds protested at the UBS headquarters, some calling UBS chairman Marcel Ospel 'Bin Ospel'. The government granted a bridging loan of 450 million francs on 3 October so that flights could resume, and a new airline is to be built around Crossair, whose stake UBS and Credit Suisse bought from SAirGroup. Lukas Mühlemann, chairman of Credit Suisse, sat on the Swissair board during its troubles. On 7 October the United States began bombing Afghanistan.
why: A national trauma: the flag carrier, a symbol of Swiss reliability, failed, and the big banks were blamed. It is the first of three moments (with UBS in 2008 and Credit Suisse in 2023) when the state had to step in for a Swiss icon.

title: America goes to war in Afghanistan
what: The United States blames the September attacks on Osama bin Laden and his group al-Qaeda, who shelter in Afghanistan. On 20 September President Bush demanded that the Taliban, who rule the country, hand bin Laden over and expel al-Qaeda; they refused. On 7 October American and British forces began bombing. On the ground they are helped by the Northern Alliance, Afghan fighters who have been at war with the Taliban for years.
why: The first answer to September 11 and the start of a twenty-year war; without it the Iraq war of 2003 has no context.

title: Euro notes and coins arrive
what: On 1 January euro banknotes and coins went into circulation in twelve countries, replacing the mark, the franc, the lira and nine other currencies, which will cease to be legal tender by the end of February. The euro has been used on currency and bond markets since January 1999 and fell against the dollar until late 2000. Switzerland keeps its franc, but Swiss travellers and shoppers across the border now meet one currency on three sides.
why: The euro becomes real for the family across the border; the currency that started weak in 1999 rises against the dollar over the following years.

title: Switzerland votes to join the United Nations
what: On 3 March Swiss voters approved joining the United Nations by 54.6 percent, with 11 full and 2 half cantons in favour, a narrow majority of the cantons. Switzerland hosts the UN's European headquarters in Geneva but has so far stayed outside the organisation.
why: Switzerland opens up, cautiously, while keeping out of the EU; neutrality is redefined, a debate that returns with the Russia sanctions in 2022.

title: Ten countries join the EU
what: On 1 May the European Union grew from 15 to 25 members: Poland, the Czech Republic, Hungary, Slovakia, Slovenia, Estonia, Latvia, Lithuania, Cyprus and Malta. Seven of them were in the Soviet bloc fifteen years ago. Switzerland must now decide whether to extend the free movement of people to the new members.
why: The reunification of Europe after 1989; cheap labour and new markets in the East for western firms, and a migration debate that reaches Britain's Brexit vote and Switzerland's 2014 initiative.

title: Bush re-elected after a campaign fought over Iraq
what: George W. Bush won a second term on 2 November with 286 electoral votes to John Kerry's 251 and 50.7% of the vote; Ohio decided it. Kerry argued that Bush had misled the country into the Iraq war, where no banned weapons had been found; Bush voters named terrorism and traditional values as what mattered most to them.
why: Every presidential election gets a beat (curator rule).

title: Greece's deficits were bigger than reported
what: On 22 November Eurostat, the EU's statistics office, published a report on Greece's budget figures, after an audit launched by the government elected in March. The deficit for 1999, the year on which Greece's entry into the euro was judged, was 3.4 percent of economic output, not 1.8 percent, and so above the 3 percent limit; for 2003 it was 4.6 percent instead of 1.7 percent. Military spending had been under-recorded and the surpluses of the social security funds overstated. Greece keeps the euro, but the reliability of its statistics is now openly questioned.
why: The first public crack in the Greek story. It changed little at the time; the Greek figures went badly wrong again in 2009.
source: Eurostat, Report on the revision of the Greek government deficit and debt figures, 22 November 2004, https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/documents/4187653/5765001/GREECE-EN.PDF (read 2026-10-04); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2004_Greek_financial_audit (read 2026-10-04)

title: The Swiss join Schengen as France and the Netherlands reject the EU constitution
what: On 5 June Swiss voters approved joining the Schengen area of passport-free travel and the Dublin asylum system by 54.6 percent. Days earlier, French voters on 29 May (55 percent) and Dutch voters on 1 June (61.5 percent) rejected the proposed European constitution, throwing the EU into a crisis about its direction.
why: Switzerland moves closer to the EU by treaty just as the EU's own voters push back; the constitution returns, renamed, as the Lisbon treaty.

title: Russia goes to war with Georgia
what: After Georgian forces moved into the breakaway region of South Ossetia on 7 August, Russia sent in troops and aircraft, drove them out and advanced into Georgia proper. A ceasefire brokered by French President Nicolas Sarkozy was agreed on 12 August. On 26 August Russia recognised South Ossetia and Abkhazia as independent states. The signs were there: Russia had held a large army exercise near the border from 15 July to 2 August, and the troops stayed there when it ended.
why: Russia's first war against a neighbour since the Soviet end; the muted Western response is the prelude to Crimea in 2014.

title: Obama is elected president
what: Barack Obama won the US presidency on 4 November with 365 electoral votes to 173 for John McCain and 52.9 percent of the vote, the first African American elected president. He takes office in January in the middle of the worst financial crisis since the 1930s and two wars.
why: Obama's first months bring the stimulus and bank stress tests; markets bottom in March 2009 and the long bull market of the 2010s follows.

title: Greece's new government finds a deficit of 12.7 percent
what: George Papandreou's party PASOK won the Greek election with 43.9 percent of the vote, and he became prime minister on 6 October. His government revealed that this year's budget deficit will be about 12.7 percent of economic output, not the 6 to 8 percent forecast before, more than four times the euro's 3 percent limit. Greece's public debt is put at about 410 billion dollars. It is the second time in five years that Greek figures have turned out far worse than reported.
why: The start of the euro crisis: markets begin to ask whether Greece can pay, and which euro country might be next. The final 2009 figure was 15.4 percent.

title: Europe bails out Greece and sets up a rescue fund
what: In late April the rating agencies cut Greek bonds to junk, half a year after Greece's new government had revealed a deficit of 12.7 percent of economic output. On 2 May the eurozone countries and the IMF agreed a 110 billion euro loan for Greece, which can no longer borrow on the markets after admitting that its deficit was far larger than reported; Greeks protested in the streets against the spending cuts attached. A week later the EU created a European Financial Stability Facility with up to 750 billion euros to stop the crisis spreading to Portugal, Spain and others. On 6 May the Dow plunged 998 points, about 9 percent, mostly within minutes, before recovering much of the loss in a 'flash crash'; the S&P 500 lost 8% in May.
why: The euro crisis begins in earnest: the S&P 500 fell 8% in May, and the Swiss franc began its rise as Europeans fled into it.

title: Ireland needs a rescue too; markets talk of the 'PIIGS'
what: On 29 November the EU and the IMF agreed a rescue for Ireland worth 85 billion euros, 67.5 billion in loans and 17.5 billion from Ireland's own reserves; up to 34 billion is for its banks. Ireland is the second euro country to need help, after Greece in May. Investors lump the weakest euro countries, Portugal, Italy, Ireland, Greece and Spain, together under the unkind nickname 'PIIGS', which the Financial Times and Barclays Capital stopped using freely this year after complaints that it is offensive.
why: The crisis spreads from one country's hidden deficits to another's bank bust; Portugal follows in spring 2011.

title: Euro summit: banks to take half off Greek debt
what: Three euro countries now live on rescue loans: Greece since May 2010, Ireland since November 2010 and Portugal since May, with 78 billion euros. In the night of 26 to 27 October euro leaders agreed that private banks will write off 50 percent of their Greek bonds, that Europe's banks must raise more capital, and that the rescue fund's firepower is to be raised to about one trillion euros. On 31 October the Greek prime minister, George Papandreou, surprised his partners by announcing a referendum on the deal. The S&P 500, which on 4 October stood about 21% below its May peak, rose 11% in October to 1,253.30, its best month since 1991.
why: Relief that the euro would hold produced the S&P 500's best month in years (+11%), with banks and miners leading; the referendum shock at month's end showed the crisis was not over.

title: Italy's borrowing costs pass 7 percent; Berlusconi and Papandreou go
what: On 9 November the interest rate on Italy's ten-year bonds rose above 7 percent, to as much as 7.45 percent, a level many economists see as unbearable; Italy's debt equals 120 percent of its economic output, and it is seen as too big to rescue with the funds available. Silvio Berlusconi resigned as prime minister on 12 November, and the economist Mario Monti was sworn in on 16 November at the head of a government of unelected experts. In Greece, George Papandreou dropped his referendum plan and resigned on 10 November; Lucas Papademos now leads a national unity government.
why: The crisis reaches one of the euro's big economies; Italian and Spanish borrowing costs stay at danger levels until Draghi's promise of July 2012.

title: Spain asks Europe to save its banks; half its young people are out of work
what: On 9 June euro finance ministers agreed to lend Spain up to 100 billion euros to recapitalise its banks, which are weighed down by failed mortgages; Bankia, the country's biggest mortgage lender, was nationalised in May and asked for 23.5 billion euros. In June the interest rate on Spain's ten-year bonds reached 7 percent. Almost a quarter of Spaniards, 24.4 percent, were unemployed in March, and among those under 25 the rate is up to 50 percent.
why: Youth unemployment becomes the human face of the crisis in Spain and Greece; a few weeks later Draghi's promise turns the tide on the markets, though not in the job centres.

title: Draghi: whatever it takes
what: Speaking in London on 26 July, the president of the European Central Bank, Mario Draghi, said that within its mandate the ECB 'is ready to do whatever it takes to preserve the euro. And believe me, it will be enough.' Borrowing costs for Spain and Italy, which had climbed to danger levels, fell after the speech.
why: The turning point of the euro crisis: the bond-buying programme announced in September is never used, but the promise ends the panic.

title: Obama wins a second term
what: Barack Obama was re-elected on 6 November with 332 electoral votes and 51.1% of the vote against Mitt Romney, holding the swing states of Ohio, Florida, Virginia and Colorado. The campaign was fought over the slow recovery from the financial crisis and Obama's health insurance law, and was the most expensive ever, with new "super PACs" spending freely.
why: Every presidential election gets a beat (curator rule).

title: Swiss voters back limits on immigration
what: On 9 February Swiss voters accepted the SVP's initiative 'against mass immigration' by 50.3 percent, a margin of 19,526 votes, and a majority of cantons. It requires quotas on immigration within three years, which contradicts the free movement of people agreed with the EU in the bilateral treaties. Brussels warned that free movement is not negotiable.
why: Puts the bilateral path in question for years; parliament later implements it without quotas, and the question of Switzerland's relationship with the EU stays open into the 2020s.

title: Ukraine's president flees after a winter of protest
what: Ukrainians have protested on the Maidan, the central square of Kyiv, since November, when President Yanukovych refused to sign an agreement with the European Union and turned to Russia, which offered 15 billion dollars and cheaper gas. From 18 to 20 February police and protesters fought in the streets; over the winter 108 protesters and 13 police officers were killed. Yanukovych fled Kyiv on the evening of 21 February, and the next day parliament voted 328 to 0 to remove him.
why: The cause of everything that follows between Russia and Ukraine: Crimea in March 2014 and the invasion of 2022.

title: Russia annexes Crimea
what: After Ukraine's pro-Russian president Viktor Yanukovych fled Kiev in February, soldiers without insignia seized Crimea's parliament and key sites. A referendum under occupation on 16 March was declared a vote to join Russia, and Russia annexed the peninsula on 18 March. The United States and the EU imposed sanctions and travel bans, and Russia was suspended from the G8.
why: The first annexation of territory in Europe since 1945 and the start of the war in eastern Ukraine; the sanctions are mild, and the full invasion follows in 2022. Review 2026-10: city name as spelled in English at the time.

title: Greeks vote No, then accept a third rescue
what: Syriza won January's election promising an end to austerity, and talks with Greece's lenders went nowhere. On 27 June Prime Minister Alexis Tsipras called a referendum on their terms; Greek banks closed, cash machines paid out no more than 60 euros a day, and on 30 June Greece became the first developed country to miss a repayment to the IMF. On 5 July 61.3 percent voted No. Yet on 13 July, after 17 hours of talks, Tsipras agreed to a third rescue with even harsher conditions than those the voters had rejected.
why: The last great scare of the euro crisis: Greece stays in the euro, and the crisis that began in October 2009 finally loses its grip on the markets.

title: Britain votes to leave the EU
what: In the referendum of 23 June, 51.9 percent of British voters chose to leave the European Union on a turnout of 72 percent. Prime Minister David Cameron announced his resignation. The pound fell to a 31-year low against the dollar and stock markets fell around the world on the day after the vote.
why: Brexit is the EU's biggest setback; the shock hit European banks hardest, Credit Suisse (-22% in June) and UBS (-17%) among them, while the S&P 500 recovered within days.

title: Trump wins the presidency
what: Donald Trump, a businessman who has never held office, won the US presidential election of 8 November against Hillary Clinton, carrying Michigan, Pennsylvania and Wisconsin, while Clinton leads in the national vote. He promises tax cuts, less regulation, infrastructure spending and tariffs. After falling overnight, US shares rose to records, led by banks: the KBW bank index gained more than 17 percent in November.
why: Polls and markets expected the opposite; the 'Trump trade' lifted banks (Citigroup +15% in November) and the dollar, and his tariffs return as a theme in 2018 and above all in 2025.

title: Pandemic: the world shuts down
what: The WHO declared a pandemic on 11 March. Italy locked down on 9 March, the United States barred travellers from Europe, and on 16 March the Swiss government declared an 'extraordinary situation', closing schools, shops, restaurants and borders; on 20 March it announced a 42 billion franc aid package. Stock markets crashed: the Dow lost 7.8 percent on 9 March, 10 percent on 12 March and 12.9 percent on 16 March, when trading was halted by circuit breakers for the third time that month and the VIX fear index closed at a record 82.69. The Fed cut rates to zero, and Congress passed a 2.2 trillion dollar relief law on 27 March; the S&P 500, 34 percent below its February record on 23 March, ended the month down 13 percent. Daimler (down 27 percent) and BMW (down 20 percent) shut their car factories, Glencore fell 38 percent, Citigroup 34 percent and General Electric 27 percent, while McDonald's served only through drive-thrus and Coca-Cola, which sells much of its drinks in restaurants and stadiums, lost 17 percent.
why: The fastest crash in the game (S&P -13% in the month, Boeing -46%, Schlumberger -50%), a political and medical event; the bottom came on 23 March.

title: Biden wins, and a vaccine works
what: Joe Biden won the US election of 3 November, with 306 electoral votes and about 51 percent of the vote, and was declared the winner by the media on 7 November; President Trump refuses to concede and claims fraud without evidence. On 9 November Pfizer and BioNTech announced that their vaccine was about 90 percent effective in trials. Investors rushed into the shares hurt most by the pandemic: Schlumberger and Glencore rose about 40%, General Electric 37%, Citigroup 33%, Daimler 30%, BMW 28% and UBS 22%, and US crude rose 27% to $45.20. The Dow closed above 30,000 for the first time on 24 November, and the S&P 500 rose 11% in the month.
why: Two answers in one week: no contested-election chaos and a way out of the pandemic. The S&P 500 gained 11%, and the losers of the lockdown soared (Boeing +46%, Credit Suisse +33%).

title: A mob storms the Capitol
what: On 6 January, as Congress met to count the electoral votes, a crowd of Trump supporters stormed the US Capitol after a rally at which the president repeated his false claims of a stolen election; five people died. Congress certified Biden's victory the next morning. The House impeached Trump for a second time on 13 January, and Joe Biden was sworn in on 20 January.
why: The low point of American democracy in the game's span; markets ignored it, but it shapes the politics of the 2024 election.

title: Bern breaks off the framework talks with the EU
what: On 26 May the Federal Council ended seven years of negotiations with the EU on an institutional framework agreement that was to bundle the bilateral treaties under common rules, saying differences over wage protection, state aid and the rights of EU citizens could not be bridged. Brussels regretted the decision and warned that existing agreements will not be updated.
why: Leaves Switzerland's EU relationship in limbo; Swiss researchers lose full access to EU programmes, and a new package is only agreed in 2024-25.

title: Russia masses troops at Ukraine's border
what: Ukraine's defence minister counted 94,300 Russian soldiers near his country's borders on 3 December. Russia, which took Crimea from Ukraine in 2014, has sent the United States and NATO two draft treaties: it wants a binding promise that Ukraine will never join NATO, and fewer NATO troops in eastern Europe. The United States warns of 'swift and severe' sanctions if Russia invades.
why: The build-up to the invasion of 24 February 2022.

title: Trump wins a second term
what: Donald Trump won the presidential election of 5 November against Vice President Kamala Harris, who replaced Joe Biden as candidate in July, with 312 electoral votes; Republicans also won the Senate. He promises tariffs, tax cuts and mass deportations. Tesla shares jumped on bets that its chief Elon Musk, who gave more than 130 million dollars to help Trump win, will benefit, and Tesla's market value passed one trillion dollars on 8 November. Tesla shares rose 38 percent in November.
why: Opens the tariff era of 2025; Tesla's +38% in November is the purest 'Trump trade' in the game, and it reversed in early 2025 when Musk's role in government hurt the brand.

title: Trump's tariffs start a trade war, and shares fall 6 percent
what: Since returning to office President Trump has put taxes on imports, called tariffs: 10% on Chinese goods from 1 February, raised to 20% on 4 March; 25% on most goods from Mexico and Canada; and from 12 March 25% on all imported steel and aluminium. Tariffs make foreign goods dearer for American buyers, and investors fear that other countries will answer with tariffs of their own. The American stock market lost 6% in March.
why: The build-up to 'Liberation Day' on 2 April, when tariffs hit the whole world.

title: Liberation Day: tariffs on the whole world
what: On 2 April President Trump announced tariffs on imports from almost every country: 10 percent for all from 5 April, and higher 'reciprocal' rates from 9 April, including 20 percent for the EU, 34 percent for China and 31 percent for Switzerland. Stock markets crashed: the S&P 500 fell 4.8 percent on 3 April and 6.0 percent on 4 April, the largest two-day loss of value in history at about 6.6 trillion dollars, and even Treasury bonds, the usual safe haven, were sold, while gold rose to a record. On 9 April Trump paused the higher rates for 90 days, and the S&P 500 jumped 9.5 percent, its biggest one-day gain since 2008; it ended April down only 1 percent. Fears of a recession knocked US crude to about 60 dollars by 8 April, the lowest since 2021, and it ended the month 17 percent lower. The Swiss rate was met with incomprehension in Bern.
why: The largest US tariff rise in nearly a century; the market fell 10% in March on tariff fear and swung wildly in April, ending the month only 1% lower, as the pause turned into deals.

title: Trump hits Switzerland with a 39 percent tariff
what: On Swiss National Day, 1 August, Washington announced a 39 percent tariff on Swiss goods from 7 August, the highest in Europe and far above the 15 percent agreed with the EU, saying Switzerland refused to make significant concessions. Federal President Karin Keller-Sutter said the Federal Council was disappointed and that the rate was far higher than the one negotiated; the machinery industry fears for tens of thousands of jobs. Pharmaceuticals remain exempt for now.
why: Switzerland's biggest trade shock in decades, a national event; it lasted until a deal in November cut the rate to 15 percent in exchange for promised Swiss investment of 200 billion dollars in the United States.
